Mr. Chairman, I shall keep the committee only a few moments while I direct attention to a case of the appointment of a postmaster, which has been placed in my hands by the national organization of the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. This concerns the appointment of Mr. A. C. Belle Isle as postmaster at Campbellton, New Brunswick. I would like to give a few details in connection with this appointment. I am informed that the vacancy occurred in January, 1932, and that several returned soldiers applied for the position, among them being Messrs. Wetmore, Jardine, Duncan, Leblanc and Boucher. The appointment was actually made in January, 1932, when it was given to the present incumbent, Mr. Belle Isle. I understand that before the appointment was actually made the position was advertised as a bilingual position, and Mr. Belle Isle was appointed as temporary postmaster, I believe in August, 1932. About six weeks later in September, 1932, a second notice was posted. The second notice was in the usual form with the exception 'that it contained the following:
Applicants must have a sufficient knowledge of both French and English to satisfactorily discharge the duties of the office.
According to the evidence of one of the civil service examiners which appears on the file, this recommendation, which I am not criticizing, was made by the Post Office Department. This matter is referred to in a letter of January 30, 1933, addressed to the Postmaster General, reading in part as follows:
It appears that, at the examination conducted by the Civil Service Commission, the outstanding candidate for this office was Mr. J. S. Wetmore, a returned soldier. There were also other returned soldiers declared qualified. It appears, however, that the English speaking
[Mr. Rhodes.)
candidates were eliminated because it was declared that they had not a sufficient knowledge of the French language.
There are two grounds for complaint in connection with this competition. The first is the manner in which the bilingual qualification wa3 advertised. We are informed that this qualification was eliminated but was ' later inserted in the advertisement in a very misleading form. Whatever the influences may be which caused the last advertisement to be posted in the manner it appeared, the impression was created in the minds of a large number of people and certainly in the minds of the English speaking returned soldier applicants that bilingualism would not be a deciding factor.
The second ground for complaint has reference to the standing of the appointee-Mr. Belle Isle. Whatever his personal qualifications are, our information indicates that his business qualifications and relationships are most unsatisfactory and should be investigated. Something in regard to his past history and standing was reported by the Civil Service Commission examiner but, for some reason, neither the Civil Service Commission nor your department conducted any further investigation, notwithstanding the examiner's recommendation that this should be done. That this candidate, whose business reputation is well known locally, should have been accepted without further investigation while qualified returned soldier applicants of unquestioned character and standing were eliminated is surprising and is the cause of great indignation.
The last paragraph reads:
In view of all the circumstances, the Canadian Legion requests that you permit this appointment to be made without reference to the bilingual qualification, as was apparently originally intended. This may entail the elimination of Mr. Belle Isle but our Campbellton branch believes this to be justified in view of his poor business standing in the community.
According to a return which was made in this house earlier in the session, the Civil Service Commission examiner recommended a further investigation into Belle Isle's character. Inquiries were made of several citizens in the community who were familiar with the appointee, including Mr. F. C. Mortimer of Saint John and Mr. H. A. Carr of Campbellton. Included in this return is a financial statement furnished by the appointee in June, 1930, for the purpose of securing credit from the Dominion Rubber Company, Limited. This purports to be an accurate and true statement of the appointee's financial position and 3hows a net surplus of $21,614. The appointee was examined under oath in October, 1931, under the provisions of the Debtors Act, and according to the evidence it is shown that the surplus which was alleged to have existed in 1930 never existed at all. The evidence which was taken under oath showed the appointee to be insolvent. There

Supply-Post Office-Outside Service
is also -on the file an affidavit by Dr. L. Erie German to the effect that -the applicant is not physically reliable for his present duty because of his addiction to certain habits which render him entirely incompetent. The Civil Service Commission examiner made a further investigation into Belle Isle's character on December 15, 1932. On January 30, 1933, the Canadian Legion wrote to the Postmaster General protesting against this -appointment. This letter also appears on the file. On February 10, 1933, the Postmaster General was interviewed by a delegation which was introduced by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). This delegation -consisted of Mr. J. C. Herwig and E. B. MacLatchy of the Canadian Legion. On February 10, 1933, a further letter was written by the legion pointing out its position in regard to this appointee. On February 21, 1933, the executive of the Campbellton branch of the legion wrote to the Postmaster General to ask that further inquiries be made with regard to -the fitness of this applicant. Under date of March 6, 1933, a letter was addressed to the Postmaster General -asking for an interview, which took place on March 7. A petition addressed to the Postmaster General and to the Prime Minister was circulated through the community. This petition reads: To the
Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, P.C., K.C., M.P.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
and
The Hon. Arthur Sauve, M.P.,
Postmaster General.
We, the undersigned, hereby strongly protest against the appointment of Mr. A. C. Belle Isle as postmaster at Campbellton, New Brunswick, and do respectfully but emphatically request that a returned soldier be appointed to this position.
The petition was signed in the course -of a few d-ays by 1,286 adults including the present mayor, four former mayors, four town councillors, the police magistrate, four lawyers, eight doctors, twenty-six merchants, twenty superintendents and firm managers, sixty semi-professional men, accountants, and so forth, and one hundred and one of the community outside the actual city of Campbellton.
The Prime Minister was interviewed with regard to the whole situation on March 31, 1933, and I understand he wrote a letter on that date to the Postmaster General asking him to look into the entire situation surrounding this appointment. I wish to -make it very clear in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister, that if in his opinion bilingual qualifications were necessary for that appointment, I am not criticizing that in the 53719-313J
slightest degree, but the information that has -been sent through the legion is to the contrary effect, namely, that bilingual qualifications were not required for the appointment in question. At the last federal election, I think that a petition to get voters in favour of Mr. Maroil was put at the post office, in order to be signed by citizens, but I asked nobody to sign it. The petition was in the part of the house where we live. I don't remember to ask anybody to sign it; and to my knowledge, Mrs. Sweetman has not asked anybody to sign it. This petition remained at our house a very 
short time. I did not see any whiskey or liquors on my premises. Mrs. Sweetman is assistant postmaster since thirty-six years, As to the oar of my son, Edwin, this one is the only owner that I know. My wife may have help him to pay, but I don't know.
The Post Office Department had no complaints against this man. Joseph Jones, who had carried the mail for four years, said that he had never heard any complaint against this post office, and1 Mr. Robert Sullivan swore:
In my opinion, the post office has always been well kept, since they had it, and never had any complaint against them.
During the past thirty-six years there has never been any reason whatever for a change. The postmaster appealed from the decision that was given. He is an Anglican, and I will read one testimonial given this man, which I think should weigh with the minister. It is a testimonial that would certainly weigh in any other part of the empire, a letter from the Lord Bishop of Quebec:
Bishopthorpe, Quebec,
August 30, 1932.
Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir,-
I take the liberty of writing to you about the post office at Port Daniel Centre, Bonaventure county, the Gaspe peninsula.
The postmaster, Mr. Edward Sweetman. has held the position for over thirty years. He is an invalid but his wife and daughter discharge the work of the office. They are people of irreproachable character and I understand from the office of the inspector at Quebec, as well as from two clergymen who have lived at Port Daniel, that the duties of the post office are carried on quite efficiently.
It is rumoured that the office is to be taken away from the Sweetmans and given to some other person.
Personally, I am and always have been a Conservative but I feel strongly that to take the office away from these worthy people would be a grave injustice. I express the hope that you will take the necessary steps in order that Mr. Edward Sweetman may be left in charge of the post office at Port Daniel Centre.
I remain,
Yours sincerely,
Lennox Quebec,
Lord Bishop of Quebec.
Now what do we find in this case? We find three applicants clamouring for the position, backed up by Dr. Paquet, and on the other hand we 'have the Lord Bishop of Quebec giving the evidence he does in this letter, backed up by the Anglican clergymen who had been in the district. Moreover, there was evidence in the possession of the department to prove that no charge had ever been made against the conduct of this post office. A returned soldier applied for the position but he was thrown aside on the ground that

Supply-Post Office-Outside Service
he had not the qualifications, being subject to fits. Mr. Ahern also applied but he too was rejected. Mr. Assels, however, was so insistent that he succeeded in getting Dr. Paquet into motion. Dr. Paquet first applied for the dismissal of Mr. Sweetman and was informed that an investigation would have to 'be held. The report of the investigator is of no significance, and it is contradicted by the postmaster himself.
I should like it to be clearly understood by the committee that the administration of the Post Office Department has become a matter of pure party patronage. In this district the postmaster had given long and efficient service, and he was highly recommended by the Bishop of Quebec. I would ask the minister also to read the evidence of Mr. Simard, and see whether the investigator was warranted in violating the act in the way he did. A petition was left at the residence of Mr. Sweetman but it was never presented to anyone; no one was ever asked to sign it either by the postmaster or by his wife. The son., who is a grown up man, owns an automobile, and as he had nothing to do with the post office he was free to come and go as he liked. No evidence was submitted against this postmaster except that Mrs. Sweetman, it is. said, made the remark on one occasion that Mr. Houde of Montreal was a tramp. That, however, is contradicted. As regards Mr. Bennett, she eulogized him, saying that if he were not clever he would not be Prime Minister.
The Postmaster General is a man of high standing in his party and enjoys a high reputation in Quebec as an honest man. I should like him to read over the evidence and say whether, in the light of the testimonial that has been given this man Sweetman and in view of the standing of these people in the community, their respectability and their long and faithful service to the department for thirty-six years, the department was justified in dismissing him simply in order to appoint a party hack who was not a returned soldier and who I am sure could not have rallied in any sense the majority of the patrons of the office. The fact of the matter is that the change was made purely for party purposes. I must leave the matter in the hands of the minister; I can do nothing now. I do hope, however, that when he has a moment of leisure the minister will look over the file and convince himself that I have made out a fair case.

I thank the hon. member for Bonaventure for his remark. I have always honoured him as a gentleman and my opinion
has not been changed to-day. With regard to the case he mentioned, it is quite true that Mr. Sweetman was dismissed upon the complaint of Mr. Paquet. The charge was denied by Mr. Sweetman but the commissioner, after holding an investigation on August 23, 1932, found the postmaster guilty on two counts. A witness Lawrence stated that Mr. Sweetman while discussing politics at his own home had declared that Mr. King was the best man and no one could be better. This same witness stated that Mr. Sweetman had stated to him that during the provincial elections of 1931, Liberal liquor had been left at his place for distribution. According to this same witness, Mr. Sweetman admitted that at the last federal elections a petition to be signed by the electors in favour of Mr. Marcil had been left at his home by his brother. The hon. member for Bonaventure knows that I have the highest respect for the bishop and the religious authorities, but this was not a matter of morals, it was one of fact. Certain regulations were enacted before my regime, and when the postmaster had been declared guilty of political partisanship, I could not do other than follow the regulations.

Did the minister take into consideration the thirty-six years of service which had been given without an adverse report being made by any officer of the department? Did the minister act merely on the opinion of a man from Rimouski who said that a petition had been left at the postmaster's house but that no one had been asked1 to sign? They could have left a similar petition at the home of the minister.
I wish to inquire from the hon. Postmaster General what decision he has reached with reference to the appointment of a postmaster for the town of Iberville?

I am aware that the hon. member for St. John's-Iberville (Mr. Rheaume) is well informed as regards this matter. A number of representations were made, as I wrote to Mr. Denicourt, one of the candidates chosen by the Civil Service Commission, and we are considering the matter. We shall have to conform to the regulations and make the appointment accordingly. It is true that it is a case which comes under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. The hon. member is well acquainted with the facts. We have to proceed with great caution, listen to representations, and when they have all been heard we shall act accordingly, conforming to the act or the public interest.
4964	COMMONS
Supply-Post Office-Outside Service

Will the hon. Postmaster General allow me to point out to him that if he wishes to conform himself to the Civil Service Act and amendments introduced by his party last year-if my memory serves me right-I cannot see why he hesitates to appoint Mr. Denicourt?
The matter is not entirely under my jurisdiction. The revenue of the post office at Iberville is more than $3,000. It is true that my approval must be sought finally.

I understand. That is why he should not have any hesitation; the Civil Service Commission has recommended the appointment of Denicourt and he has his appointment in his pocket since April 3. On April 19, 1933, I wrote the following letter to the hon. Postmaster General: Hon. Arthur Sauve,
Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Ont.
Hear Sir,-
I have been informed that the Civil Service Commission had chosen Mr. Wilfrid Denicourt as postmaster of Iberville, over fifteen days ago, but his appointment had not yet been approved by the Post Office Department.
I have no doubt that the department will approve the appointment of Mr. Denicourt because he is a returned soldier and qualified for the position.
I am aware that influences were brought to bear to appoint another person, however, I trust that nothing will come of it, because it would be very unfair to Mr. Denicourt and, furthermore, your department cannot disregard the Civil Service Commission's choice. I am in no way interested in this appointment. All that I request is that the act should take its course.
The following is the answer received from the Postmaster General, on April 20, 1933: Dear Mr. Rheaume,-
I am in receipt of your letter dated April 19 with reference to Mr. Wilfrid Denicourt who, as you stated was chosen to be postmaster at Iberville.
In reply, I wish to state that my department is awaiting the inspector's report to settle the appointment permanently.
If, my memory serves me right, there are two returned soldiers who have applied for the position.
As you are also aware, the new Civil Service Commission is not complete.
According to the examination list Mr. Denicourt came first with 84 points and Mr. de Beaujour is fifth out of six candidates, with 71 points. I trust that the hon. Postmaster General will approve the choice of the Commission. The latter when advertising the vacant position stated:
The secretary .of the commission will receive applications up to February 17, 1933.
 '
According to the report, before me, from the commission, five candidates out of six complied to that order of the commission; the only one who did not comply was Mr. de Beaujour, who forwarded his application on March 10. I cannot see why one should hesitate in appointing Mr. Denicourt who is a returned soldier, has five children and has had no work for over a year, while Mr. de Beaujour has been employed over 3 years at the locks in St. John; he earns $450 to $500 per year and draws a pension of $175 from the State. Moreover, he owns a lot where he has a garden. He therefore, is fairly well-to-do. Denicourt is a returned soldier, a brave lad who joined the 22nd Battalion, passed the Civil Service test and came out first. Mr. de Beaujour came out 5th; however, I am aware that he has been pulling strings and the hon. Postmaster is aware of that fact. When Mr. Goyette died, last autumn, Mr. Ernest Thuot, a good conservative, probably the most Conservative partizan in the county of St. John's-Iberville-

There are not many in St. John's-Iberville?
Mr. RHEAUME (Translation) -who has been head clerk at the Liquor Commission,, ever since the store was open in Iberville, gave up his position to become temporary postmaster, if I am well informed, Thuot wants de Beaujour to be appointed on condition that he is kept on and that the salary and pension be split in two. I consider that Thuot's appointment was not regular and did not comply with the act. I can assure you that if ever the Liberal party returns to-powTer the first dismissal will be that of the postmaster at Iberville. I shall request it myself as an act of justice. Mr. Thuot had no business to give up his position at the Liquor Commission. He had been employed there for the last five or six years. He took an active part in politics, in 1931, he went to-the county of Rouville-when employed at the Quebec Liquor Commission to carry on conservative propaganda from door to door. The Quebec government did not even hold an inquiry about it. After the death of Mr. Goyette he gave up his position and deprived MisS Goyette of the position she had held at the post office for over twenty years, and threw-her on the street. To-day, if Denicourt is not appointed, it is because influence was-brought to hear to have de Beaujour appointed in his place, so as to keep Thuot there and divide the salary. If Thuot lost his position he, has but himself to blame and- I do not think that he can get that position, back at the Quebec Liquor Commission.

Supply-Post Office-Outside Service
I trust that, notwithstanding all the recrimination I have heard, the Postmaster General will comply with the act as regards this appointment. I wish to inquire from him after these explanations-he knows the facts as well as I do-whether he will accept the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission in connection with this appointment.
I think the hon. member will be satisfied when the case is definitely settled.

I hope so. Now, sir, I do not wish to hold up the estimates, but I would request the hon. Postmaster General to state why, in the parish of St. Georges-dTIenriville, county of Iberville, two tenders were called in connection with the rural mail contract, when a third contract was awarded without calling for tenders.
May I request the hon. member to kindly postpone his inquiry as I have not the information with me. It is a question of contracts and there are many of them.
There are but two.

I mean throughout Canada. St. John's-Iberville is but one county and there are many others. I shall be pleased to give him all the explanations and details he desires. I do not wish to conceal anything, he has a right to receive the information, and he shall have it.

Thanks.
However, I would not like to have these details after the contract has been awarded.
No, no.

May I
Inquire from the hon. Postmaster General why a contract was awarded without tenders being called and why tenders are necessary in the other case?
At present, I cannot answer. Had I this information I would willingly give it.
When does the hon. minister expect to furnish this information.
I shall be able to give it on Monday morning.

This will
be quite satisfactory. Now, sir, a contract held by Mr. Barriere, in St. Gregoire, was transferred. Can the hon. postmaster inform me to whom this contract was transferred?

I have not the name of the person here. The hon. member should have notified me that he desired this information; he could, in the course of the session, have secured that information either by putting a question on the order paper or otherwise. He would have 'been given a reply in the house, and, thereby, had it inserted in Hansard. I would have 'been pleased to have given the information as that is one of the aims of the session. We cannot furnish all information without knowing what hon. members require. I shall make a point to bring such information with me, on Monday morning.

I would
like to know to whom the contract of Mr. Barriere of St-Gregoire-le-Grand has been transferred. I would also like to know why, in the same parish, two calls for tenders were posted, from March 27 to April 22, and why one of these posters was taken down. I think that one of these contracts was awarded to Mrs. Bessette of St-Gregoire-le-Grand.

There was
correspondence exchanged recently in this connection,

Will the
hon. Postmaster General furnish me with this information Monday morning?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, western Canada is not the only place where English speaking postmasters were appointed in parishes entirely French Canadian. In my own county, adjacent to Ottawa, the thing was done a little over a year ago. In January, 1931, the postmaster of Val-des-tBois was dismissed because of political partisanship.
What parish?

Val-des-Bois, Hull county. On January 22, four applications were made to the Civil Service Commission by Messrs. Archie Larocque, Theodore Thibeault, Hermas Morin and Isidore Larocque. Some time later, after the position had been advertised, three candidates were given a test and Mr. Peck was appointed. He was the least qualified candidate, according to the report of the inspector who had charge of the test.
Representations were made to the Postmaster General. In the file which I have here, there is a memo from the Deputy Postmaster General, Mr. Gaboury:
The Postmaster General has received further representations concerning the above postmaster-
Private Bills

ship. Provided the assistant postmaster can take care of the bilingual requirements of the office, the appointment of Mr. Peck will be satisfactory.
However the examiner or inspector who had charge of the test refused to recommend the appointment of Mr. Peck because at Val-des-Bois, there is only one English speaking citizen and that is Mr. Peck; the entire population with this exception speak French. On April 23, Mr. Underwood wrote to the district superintendent:
Representations have been received by the Postmaster General concerning applicant Peck who, it is noted, is not considered by the investigating officer as having the necessary bilingual qualifications.
This matter has been examined and the department considers that, provided the assistant postmaster can fully take care of the bilingual requirements of the office, there would appear to be no objection to Mr. Peck's appointment if he is otherwise a recommendable applicant.
Mr. Peck does not speak a word of French. There is not an English family at Val-des-Bois. The commission requested on more than one occasion

Order!
It is six o'clock.

I shall be through in a minute. On more than one occasion the commission requested a report from the district superintendent. It took four months to obtain that report, and, finally, Mr. Peek was appointed. I take this opportunity to point out this affair to the house. I think, sir, that in the county of Hull, where there are few English speaking citizens, and at Val-des-Bois, in particular, where there are none, the department should have appointed a French speaking postmaster.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, there was a postal station on St. John street in Quebec which was closed recently, and I have received many letters and resolutions protesting against the closing. Would the hon. gentleman say what were the reasons which induced him to make that change?

The reason is that the closing of that
postal station on May 1 will result in an immediate saving of about $1,800 per annum. The ultimate saving through the withdrawal of the staff and subsequent adjustments will amount to about $5,000 per annum. At the same time we are improving the service by two suboffices.

I must tell my hon.
friend that the people of that section of the city do not seem to agree with him as to the improvement resulting from this change, because I am receiving many protests about it. This post office is situated in one of
the most important sections of the city of Quebec. The citizens of both Quebec South and Quebec East were taking advantage of the facilities there. However, I hope if the result is not what my hon. friend expects, it will be possible to persuade him to revert to the former situation.

We will see at the end of
this year. I myself received several protests, but I sent letters to the Quebec papers explaining our purpose, and after the explanation given I think my hon. friend from Quebec East will accept our action. I did not receive any further protests since.

We 'have much good
will for the minister.

I have a complaint from Dease Lake and Telegraph Creek post offices in British Columbia. A notice has been posted in those post offices that from now on the parcel post rate will be 12 cents a pound. They are the only places in British Columbia where that change has been made.
I have inquired as to the reason. I realize it is probably for the sake of economy, but I would like to ask the Postmaster General how much he anticipated will be saved by depriving those two post offices of that service. It is 5 cents a pound in other post offices in British Columbia, but it is raised to a flat rate of 12 cents for those two post offices. I have taken it up with the deputy minister but he could not give me any other answer than that it is done for the sake of economy. I can see no warrant for depriving those people of that convenience for the few dollars that may be saved; for I presume the mail has to go there anyway, whether there are few parcels or many, and I cannot see what saving can be accomplished.

We tried to do our best;
if we have not satisfied the people there we will seek to do so. But my hon. friend will understand the situation that faces us on account of the depression of business. We are trying bo do our best to serve the public and at the same time to serve the interests of the country. If your people are not satisfied we will seek to satisfy them.

May I also ask
the Postmaster General this: in the same district the towns of Anyox and Alice Arm up to last spring had three mail services a week. Last spring they were cut to two, which was naturally a hardship on	those	communities.	The latest report that I have
received informs me that it is anticipated that the service will be put to once a week.
4968	COMMONS
Supply-Post Office-Outside Service
1 have several letters containing these complaints, but I do not think it is necessary to put them on record. I just want to register these complaints and I should like the minister to look into the matter very carefully before reducing the services from three to one a week. The population is the same as it was before, so I do not see why they should be deprived of that service.
We have asked for a better price for a weekly service. I suppose we will receive tenders, and we shall do our best.

Can the
hon. Postmaster General recall the facts in connection with the postoffice of Missanabie, county of Algoma, Ontario, which were the subject of quite a considerable correspondence between the Rev. Father Maynard, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and the hon. Postmaster General? The hon. Postmaster General, I presume,, recalls this post office and can reply to the questions which I desire to put to him?
Yes.

Will the
hon. Postmaster inform the house who is, at present, in charge of this post office?
Missanabie? Mr. Stuart.
It is the same Mr. Stuart who was the subject of the correspondence referred to?
I think so.
Evidently, the Postmaster considers that Mr. Stuart has the qualifications necessary to fill this important post?	Silence is consent.

I beg your pardon! I was waiting for the hon. member to resume his seat before replying. I am still working on that case. We have done our utmost to settle it, endeavouring at the same time to protect the interest of the department and meet the wishes of people of Missanabie, in Algoma West. There are naturally two sides to this question of a postmaster. Charges were lodged against him because of his personal views and behaviour towards certain citizens. The charges were absolutely denied by the postmaster. We notified the district superintendent to look into this matter and hold an inquiry. The superintendent sent in a report stating that the charges against this postmaster were not substantiated. Moreover, I requested one of the higher officials of the department Mr. 
Underwood, who is General Superintendent of Postal Services, to make a thorough examination of this case and continue the inquiry in this respect. Mr. Underwood's report is as follows-
Would the hon. minister give the date?
September 16, 1932.
Was there a report made after that date?

I do not think so. The report is as follows:
The undersigned discussed this question with the district superintendent, at North Bay. The Inspector Gagne who made the latest report on the case, was not at the office, I could not question him personally on the matter.
The district superintendent is of the opinion that there is no justification to take any definite action against that postmaster, considering the complaints lodged up to date. He added that there were no doubt people around Missanabie who are inimical to the postmaster and who are making every effort to have him dismissed.
On the other hand, the district superintendent considers that the efficient services rendered by the postmaster and the satisfactory way he manages the post office from the financial viewpoint, etc., justifies his maintenance in office. So far as we are specially concerned, namely, that an assistant postmistress unsealed a letter, it is clear that she did not do so with premeditation or malice. Had she acted thus, she could no doubt have destroyed this letter, while it has been clearly established that the moment she noticed that she had unsealed this letter, by mistake, thinking it was addressed to the postmaster, she immediately handed the letter to the son of the person to whom the letter was addressed, so that he might deliver it, explaining what had happened; moreover, the letter was never taken out of the envelope.
It was stated that the postmaster was hostile to French Canadians. This statement is denied by the postmaster who says that he gets along very well with the majority of the people but that there are some who spread trouble and discord and endeavour to bring charges against him. The present case is an instance of a case where it is difficult to get to the bottom of the affair; however, after discussing the subject with the district superintendent, who has personal knowledge of the facts, and considering how far the affair has gone, I think that we are not justified in taking immediate action by dismissing this postmaster.
(Signed) E. J. Underwood,
General Superintendent of Postal Services.
The hon. Postmaster, I think, stated that this report was dated May 16, 1932?
September.

September 1932?

Supply-Post Office-Outside Service
Yes.

If I
understood the wording of this report, it is stated that action cannot be taken immediately? We are now in May, 1933; it is evident that no action was taken immediately. When does the hon. Postmaster General expect to take energetic action, in keeping with the actual situation as represented to the hon. Postmaster General?

Energetic
action? I do not wish people to think that I lack energy; however, I should like to be given credit for sound judgment. It is not a matter of energy only but of sound judgment.	.

It is an
excellent thing to have both.

Yes, one
must have both. Since that date there has been some correspondence exchanged with Father Maynard, who seems quite unfriendly towards the postmaster. I inquired from the local member, who should be consulted in such matters, and he informed me that the postmaster enjoyed the confidence of the great majority of the citizens of that locality.

Who is
the member for that constituency?
It is Mr. Simpson, member for Algoma West. The hon. member for Quebec East must be acquainted with him.

There is
nothing wrong in asking his name.

No, on the
contrary. If some one inquired who was the member for Quebec East, everybody would know that it is the Hon. Mr. Lapointe.

The hon.
member for Quebec East robbed me of my powder 1

I wish to state to the hon. senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) that, ever since then, we have received no request from any group of persons belonging to the constituency, protesting against his conduct and asking for his resignation.
As to the administration of this post office by Mr. Stuart-the report speaks for itself-[DOT] there are no complaints. Mention was made of a letter unsealed by an assistant. She gave an explanation, which is, moreover, that given by many postmasters. Furthermore, even under the preceding regime, I have knowledge 53719-314
of similar cases happening, and the then Postmaster General did not consider it sufficient, after listening to explanations given, to demand the resignation of the postmaster.

The hon.
Postmaster .General is not quite consequent. Perhaps, he wishes, in his argument, to resort to the premises which he laid down just now, when he stated that not energy but sound judgment was needed.

No, both
energy and sound judgment.

I always
thought that, first, sound judgment was needed and, then, energy. At all events, the hon. Postmaster General states that no complaints have been received for a year past. It is unnecessary to have received complaints within a year; positive complaints were lodged and the correspondence is there to prove it. The Rev. Father Maynard openly complained of the administration of that post office in bitter terms, perhaps, not without cause. The Hudson Bay's representative also complained. An inquiry was held. The hon. Postmaster states that it is all over, that a report was made in September, 1932, and immediate action was to be taken. It is unnecessary to sift the whole affair again and to hear further complaints. It behooves the Postmaster General to act so as to arrive at some conclusion. This place, sir, is situated in the county of Algoma which is worthily represented in the house by the chief whip of the party on your right, sir, that is, perhaps, an explanation. However, faced with these specific charges which were lodged by the Rev. Father Maynard and others, I think that the Postmaster General shows much indolence and a great lack of energy. Perhaps, there is some sound judgment mingled with it, however, as the matter stands, it does not show very much.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a situation which exists no doubt throughout Canada, but which does exist in that part of Canada west of the great lakes. Because of this reduction in railway service we are receiving a rather limited postal service. The branch line upon which I happen to live was built some twenty years ago. Originally we had a passenger train and a mixed train daily with a daily .mail delivery both east and west. This service has since been reduced to tri-weekly. There are other instances where the service has been reduced to bi-weekly. Because of these reductions in service the business men of the communities find themselves without the necessary postal accommodation, and I was wondering if it would be possible for the Post Office Department to consider the possibility of putting on a truck or automobile service in order to provide the necessary postal accommodation. The Post Office Department
is not responsible for the situation which has been created by the railways. In some cases where the railway service has been cut we have put on a special service and I hope that within a few months the situation of which my hon. friend complains will be remedied.

I wish to say a few words that may not be strictly in order on this vote but I think I can say them in a shorter time than might be spent wrangling over a point of order. I wish to call the attention of the house to the indefensible waste of public money in having two fully equipped independent post offices in this building, within ten feet of each other. I wonder where anywhere in the whole world you could find a parallel condition. The most easterly one has a clientele at the most of ninety-six, and very often, as the records show, of not more than fifty, with perhaps a dozen officials as well. We have in our post office sufficient men who are competent to do the whole thing. The saving may not amount to more than $10,000, and $10,000 out of $345,000,000 is not a very big item, but it is the look of the thing. In these days of low incomes and high taxation people look at that sort of thing and they do not like it. It is the sort of thing that might suddenly sweep the country. Suppose some of the C.C.F. went about the country saying: "These two old parties have been perpetrating a thing like that for the last thirty years." A British government was defeated on a snap vote on a question of cordite. It was a trivial thing, there was no war on at the time, but there was a sudden flare-up and the government was defeated. It is the appearance of the thing I want to get at. If we allow these things to go on right under our nose, it will be argued, what will we do in bigger things. I am not saying anything against any official; I am simply saying that one post office would be ample for both houses.	*

However, I always wonder whether the power of dismissal of the Postmaster General, which is quite extensive, is not out-weighed by his power of reinstatement of those whe were dismissed. Much of the evidence is contradicted by affidavits, however, I do not intend to refer again to that particular phase. When the hon. When was he reinstated? In what year?

He was
dismissed about 1924, after a thorough inquiry.
In what year was he reinstated?

He was reinstated in 1931. If I ask this question, it is because I am aware that the hon. Postmaster General has a very generous disposition and that if any document in the file escaped his eye, he may have an opportunity to verify the facts and act accordingly.

Had the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard) drawn my attention to this matter in 1931, I would have sifted the case thoroughly and given him an answer. I promise him to thoroughly examine this case and shall give him an answer next time.

1 have another case that I would like to bring to the attention of .the minister. This is in connection with the post office at Alvena, Saskatchewan. The postmaster at this office was charged with political partisanship by the defeated Conservative candidate on October 8, 1930. The postmaster denied the charge and furnished declarations to that effect, but he was later dismissed in spite of this and in spite of the report of the district superintendent in which he says:
I circulated the patrons of the Alvena office on November 14, asking for an expression of opinion as to service rendered and whether or not the charges made were correct. To date sixty replies have been received, and of the patrons responding forty-six have expressed satisfaction with Mr. Slusar and his conduct of the office. The remaining fourteen claim that Mr. Slusar is not capable of handling the business since the post office has assumed new importance. He is said to be very slow in the sorting of mail and writing of money orders, owing to bis lack of education, and to be, at times, disobliging and impolite. Complaint has also been made as to the present location of the office, which is across the railway tracks from the rest of the village.
The inspector was sent out, and the report further states:
In several replies to my circular-

The superintendent had sent out circulars to the various patrons of the office.
-it was intimated that the complainants were making an effort to have Mr. Slusar removed from his position so that they, or some one of them, might obtain charge of the office, and that Mr. Peter Drabinasty, garage man, was the leader of this agitation. This seems borne out by the fact that several replies to my circular are in this man's handwriting although signed by different parties. The same implication was made to Mr. Cumming,-
That is the inspector.
-and it was suggested by Mr. Dmetro Andrunyk, general merchant, and Mr. J. Gray, agent of the Searle Elevator Company (both considered to be men of dependable judgment) that it would be doubtful if a change for the better could be made at the present time on account of the general character of the persons available for the position. Experience has shown that the postmaster in a community of this kind is particularly the target for criticism.
Further on in his report the superintendent says:
I am doubtful if the present postmaster will prove able to rise to the responsibilities of this office and provide satisfactory service for the business of the growing village, but I think that no action should be taken against him at the present time.
That is the report of the district superintendent. I may say from my own personal knowledge of this particular office and the community that the report is quite correct. I know that when they did appoint a successor ,to this postmaster he was not as well able to carry on the business of the office as the previous postmaster. But in spite of this report of the superintendent an investigation was ordered into the charges of political partisanship, and the commissioner who held the investigation was again in this case, as in the case of the Jansen post office, the brother of the defeated Conservative candidate. Evidence was taken by this commissioner, and two witnesses were called. One mentioned that when he heard the remarks of the postmaster which were the basis of the charge of partisanship there were two men present whose names 'he mentioned, and who had heard the remarks at the same time. After the evidence was taken the postmaster secured declarations from these two men who were supposed to have heard him make the remarks, and forwarded them to the Post Office Department, and both men in their declarations say that the evidence given was incorrect. They both say:
I was at no political meeting at any time in Alvena during 1930 and at no time did the said Slusar talk politics to me or in my presence.

This, as I have said, was sent to the Postmaster General, and he was asked by the commissioner for advice as to whether further investigation, should be made. On May 12 a letter was sent to the commissioner, and there was no reply to that, but in spite of the production of new evidence and the desire of the postmaster to have it considered the order was issued that the postmaster should be dismissed and another man appointed in his place. I would like to ask the Postmaster General if he did give consideration to those declarations, which practically nullify all the evidence that was taken before the commissioner, and if he did after consideration of those declarations decide that there should be no further investigation?

Mr. Slusar was dismissed on
the charge of political partisanship. The charge was denied by the postmaster and was investigated by Commissioner Wilson on the 29th of April, 1931. He was found guilty on four counts: that the postmaster made partisan remarks among a number of persons at a meeting held in Alvena in the interests of the Conservative candidate for the purpose of inducing them to support the Liberal candidate; that the postmaster tried to induce persons to support the Liberal candidate; that the postmaster in the winter of 1930-31 at his store premises in the presence of at least three persons attacked the present administration with the intent of affecting the political views of persons present; and that during the provincial election campaign in 1929, on the store and post office premises the postmaster pointed out to an elector the advisability of voting for the Liberal party. He consequently was found guilty by the commissioner, and I followed the rule established by my predecessors. As to the new postmaster, I must say that the question raised by the hon. member is occupying the attention of the department, and we will continue to give attention to and review the case.

The hon. minister has not got my point at all. Perhaps in trying to be brief I have not put it very clearly. The minister just gave a review of the charges and the evidence heard and the finding of the commissioner. I was asking if the minister did consider the declarations that were sent in by the two men who had been stated by one witness as having been present and heard these remarks alleged to have been made by the postmaster. They denied that they had been present at the meeting, which to my mind absolutely nullifies the evidence given by the

one witness. Did the Postmaster General give any consideration to that fact?

Yes, I understand that is what happened, and I understand that the former postmaster has made a complaint against the acting postmaster. The case of the former postmaster is settled; he has been replaced. However, in view of what has been said with regard to the administration of the new postmaster, we are disposed to review the case to see if we cannot satisfy my hon. friend.

I know the former postmaster was dismissed; I did not need to be told that. I am trying to find out why he was dismissed. No, no! I have still further questions to ask. I wish to inquire from the hon. Postmaster General whether he was acquainted with a person named Emile Bourre, an ex-employee of the post office, in Montreal, but superannuated in 1931, and to whom leave of absence, with full salary, was granted, before being superannuated.
I am not personally acquainted with Mr. Bourre and I cannot answer this question the way it is put, I have not the details with me.

I regret very much that the hon. Postmaster General has not the details with him because I am informed that Mr. Bourre bad a leave of absence for 720 days, with full salary, on the recommendation of the Deputy Postmaster General. I cannot vouch for the fact, I received the information through the mail. I cannot vouch for it as a fact. A letter received informs me that this chap was given 720 days leave of absence. He must be some kind of friend.
I have been requesting, sir, since April 19, from the hon. Postmaster General, the information which he gave me just now, be made a statement with reference to the dismissal of postmasters under various governments, he quietly passed over Louis Philippe Pelletier's mournful reign at the Post Office Department, when the guillotine was in constant motion.

And when I inquired as to the dismissals of postmasters since August, 1930-the house having ordered the tabling of this information- his duty was to give the full information and there was no need of going back to 1896, while at the same time leaving a wide gap between 1911 and 1921. I have remained faithful to the great leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and I recall how he reprimanded the then Postmaster General in 1911.

I am not going to discuss what has already been debated in the house. I found quite an interesting document in the patent records. It is the description of the letter box, the famous box, a marvel of Amedee Lesieur, patented under another name. Amedee Lesieur, I stated the other day, was a wine merchant of Montreal, who had carried on a profitable business when the Scott Act was in force in Quebec; now he is a manufacturing agent, an agent of applicants for patents. You are aware, sir, that pure water is called in pharmaceutics aqua pura and that under that term a druggist always asks a higher price for a bottle of aqua pura than for an ordinary glass of water. I also am aware that chemists designate it as H20; it is a chemical formula which means water-pure water as obtained from a tap just like the water the Prime Minister sent, at the expense of the state, to Washington for the use of the Kiwanis club. That is called, sir, diplomatic water, it is a special water. However, the following is the description of the famous box of which you have a photograph under your eyes, that stove pipe which is described as if it were the eighth marvel of the world.
When the description of this stove pipe is read to you, sir, you will imagine it is made of platinum, with gold supports, covered with rubies and similar to the ancient jewels found in Tut-Ank-Ahmon's tomb. Allow me to read to you the marvellous description of Amedee Lesieur's box:
No. 319.598. Mail Box. Boite postale.
Alfred Edmund Guy Madiey, Westmount, Quebec, Canada, 9th February, 1932. Filed 3rd December, 1931. Serial No. 384,322.
1.	A rural mail box comprising a cylindrical casing closed at one end-
It is no longer a stovepipe closed at one end; it has become a cylindrical casing.
-and open at the other end-
As all stove pipes are.
-a hingedly mounted door for the open end, combined reinforcing and spring actuated supporting means for the box.
Is that not marvellous?
2.	A rural mail box comprising a cylindrical casing with a pivotally mounted door-
One is a hingedly mounted door and is a pivotally mounted door.
-at one end and closed at the other end, a bendable metallic band adapted to envelop and reinforce the box-
Apparently the box is reinforced at both ends.
-and having one end suitably bent, a standard provided with a cap having an opening therein, a retaining bolt spring pressed for engagement with the band and with the standard and a tensioning nut for said bolt.
So there is a nut for the bolt. This is very important, very difficult ,and very highly technical.
3.	In a rural mail box and in combination, a cylindrical casing closed at one end and provided with a gravity-operable door-

So we have three doors, the hingedly mounted door, the pivotally mounted door and now the gravity operable door.
-at the other end, a standard, a combined reinforcing and supporting member for the casing and pivotal spring pressed means connecting said member with the standard.
Is that not marvellous? Is it not a grand thing for which to grant $28,000 to this fellow? Mark you, sir, that the report of the Postmaster General is dated November 5, 1931. He speaks of the scarcity of rural mail boxes in the maritime provinces and in Quebec, and he goes on to say:
This box is a greatly improved one, is patented and cannot be purchased elsewhere, and is particularly adapted to use in the postal service. The minister states that the price of $2.75 is fair and reasonable.
I am sure the minister has never seen the box; he has only seen the description. The descriptions of the three doors are worth a dollar each; this man was a marvel to make such a wonderful thing for 25 cents less than the $3.

The same question was put to each of the candidates, to Voisine and Cote: Will you change the site of the post office, if you are appointed? Reply of Mr. Cote:	"No."
Reply of Mr. Voisine: "No." That is, the site was to be the same, in both cases. Yet, it was contended that the site suggested by Mr. Cote was unsuitable while the one suggested by Mr. Voisine was a suitable one. And an official, so important as Mr. Underwood wrote to Mr. Green, of Quebec, to request him to change the rating of Cote because he had offered an unsuitable site, when this site was exactly the same as the one offered by Voisine. What what was the rating of Voisine? Ninety per cent. Dominique Cote, 85 per cent. However, note, sir, that it *was said then that Voisine was offering a suitable site while Cote was offering a rather unsuitable one. For Voisine, it was said: "Private residence, very good accommodation." For Cote: "Private residence, poor accommodation."
This was evidently the reason for which the rating of Voisine was 90 per cent while that of Cote was 85 per cent.
Now, sir, what was the second report sent? I had all the trouble in the world to lay my hand on the first report of Mr. Green. I was obliged to have motion after motion adopted, and I had to write many a time to the Postmaster General and his officials, so as to obtain this report. Why is this information, which is requested by members who have a right to it, not given with good grace by the hon. Postmaster General? I have here the second report referring to Voisine and Cote:
Thomas Voisine: Class C, married, age 52; residence in "the" district 12; service overseas, no; education, primary; speaks, reads and writes French, but no English; has the candidate himself the required qualifications to perform efficiently the duties of this position, yes; character, very good; habits, very good; reputation, very good; what experience has the candidate had which may enable him to fill this position? None, except as temporary postmaster; other experience, secretary to the municipality of Ste-Rose.
Dominique Cote:
Class B, bachelor, age 35; residence in the district 35; service overseas, yes; education, primary; speaks, reads and writes French, but not English; has the candidate himself the required qualifications to perform efficiently the duties of that position? yes; character, very good; habits, very good; reputation, very good; what experience has the candidate had which may enable him to fill this position? none; other experience, always been a labourer.
The two candidates were questioned.
Rating: Thomas Voisine, 90 per cent; Dominique Cote, 75 per cent.

That is, in the second report it was no more stated that Cote offered an unsuitable site, which was untrue, the first time. The qualifications of the two candidates were the same with this difference that one, Cote, was a returned soldier, and that the other, Voisine, was not, and the rating of Voisine is left at 90 per cent, while the rating of Cote is reduced from 85 per cent to 75 per cent. That is, according to Mr. Underwood, when the Postmaster General stated that Cote had offered an unsuitable site, he had 85 per cent; when he offers a suitable site, he is reduced to 75 per cent. The report continues:
The post office is no more in a public building, but in a separate one and a very good site. Even if there is no change.
Each candidate is willing to devote all his time to the duties which the post office necessitates. Voisine intends to obtain the help of his son and daughter and Cote the help of Miss Blanche Landry, who has had six years of postal experience.
Moreover, that is how post offices are kept in rural sections.
Do you consider this candidate sufficiently qualified as regards education, experience, personal qualifications, character, honesty, also do the premises and site answer the requirements of the post office in question?
Answer: yes. in both cases.

This is what happened. Instead of submitting the case to the Civil Service Commission, the Postmaster General listened to the recommendations or gossip which came from three unqualified individuals of Notre-Dame-du-Lac.
The hon. Postmaster General wrote to me as follows, on July 13, 1932:
The superintendent has forwarded together with his report a letter from Mr. Cote, a photographed copy of which I am sending you, it gives a good idea of the education of this candidate. You will no doubt, be of my opinion, that the Postmaster General cannot entrust the postal administration, especially when it is a matter of such importance as the post office of Notre-Dame-du-Lac, to a candidate who has no experience in office work and who, judging from his writing, is not capable of personally taking charge of the post office.
And the Postmaster General sends me a photostat of a letter from the returned soldier Cote, of Notre-Dame-du-Lac. I replied to the Postmaster General that his writing was better than his or mine.
Another case. According to a return tabled recently, may I inquire what was decided with reference to the person who was appointed postmaster at Coaticooke? It is a much more important post office than.
Notre-Dame-du-Lac. The Coaticooke post office has a revenue of $5,255 per year.

There were ten other candidates. However, this chap, who was not qualified was appointed. The Postmaster General will contend that he was appointed by the Civil Service Commission. That is true. But, on the other hand, the Postmaster General accepted from the Civil Service Commission the appointment of an uneducated person, as postmaster of an office which has a revenue of $5,255 per year; yet he finds that a candidate considered sufficiently educated by an inspector, is unfit to take charge of a post office with a revenue of $900 per year.
As to the rating, the following is what the Deputy Minister wrote himself to the Civil Service Commission. Return No. 65 S-P. 192:
The department does not assume that the commission is bound to accept as unquestionable the rating given by the district superintendent of postal service. The department has had sufficient experience to know that this is not the case.
There is a complaint in connection with the Coaticooke post office and I trust that, in future, the hon. Postmaster will conform to the act when it is a question of making appointments or dismissals and that he will guard himself against doing an injustice and, moreover, not come to the house boasting like the Pharisees of the good deeds done and the prayers said.
The hon. Postmaster seems to have every theological virtue and all those that man may have inherited since Adam. That is splendid, but sounds like the Pharisees. It is much better to be a publican and not boast so much. The hon. Postmaster General would have been better advised to allow the members to give credit for good deeds rather than have him behead certain postmasters of their country. It would have been better for them to defend him when he was attacked. I think that it would have been more proper and decent for the party's sake that the members who requested the Postmaster General to be unjust, to rise themselves and defend his attitude. Perhaps,
Supply-Post Office

many things were requested from the minister, which he now regrets and hon. members have not the courage to rise in the house and defend him.
I wish to state to the hon. Postmaster General: If he wishes to retain the esteem of our English speaking fellow-citizens in the Cabinet, the House of Commons and throughout the country, he should take as his motto these few words said by the most eminent of all French Canadians, Sir Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine: "Let us assert our rights." Let us prove our courage, let us never be intimidated by the cries of fish-hawks which fanatics set up all over the country. Fanaticism is of short duration. When an appeal is made to hatred of race, language and religion, sooner or later, it is certain to cause a revolution. Let one recall that in 1917 the election was made against Quebec, that the Union Cabinet denounced Quebec in every part of Canada and, four years later, it was Quebec who gave the majority to the party which triumphed.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the house any longer, I stated part of what I had to say, I set aside much because we arc nearing the end of the session; however, I would request the government to see that the injustice perpetrated by the Post Office department be atoned and that it be courageous enough to refuse the requests of its partizans who are not, themselves called upon to defend the government. I trust that, in the future, they will better defend it, that no more injustice will be perpetrated against the French or English speaking Canadians, and that the Postmaster General will act so as to be equally respected by both French and English speaking Canadians.

Before this item is carried, I wish to suggest to the Postmaster General some means to make amends for the wrong done to Mr. Carrier, ex-postmaster of Levis. It goes without saying that the Postmaster General was unfair to this man. He knew that his services had always been of the best, that his conduct was above reproach, that nothing could be said against him from a political viewpoint and, he was aware that in retiring from the service, Mr. Carrier, the latter could not enjoy a pension. I would request the hon. Postmaster General, so as to make amends for the wrong done, to reimburse him the contribution he made to the superannuation fund, beside the gratuity already paid to him. I trust that the hon. Postmaster General wishes to do a kind act before retiring for the night 
and that he will think over my suggestion and carry it out.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
